definition:
The Bible's story can be told as the story of God making a home with his people. God is present everywhere, since “heaven, the highest heaven, cannot contain You” (1 Kings 8:27), but Scripture also speaks of a special, covenanted presence: God dwelling in a particular place so that his people can meet him, worship him, and be forgiven. That presence runs from the garden of Eden to the tabernacle Israel carried through the wilderness, to the temple Solomon built in Jerusalem, and then, in the New Testament, to Jesus, who spoke of his body as a temple, and to the church, which Paul calls God's temple by the Spirit. The Bible ends with a city that has no temple, because God and the Lamb fill it. This study follows the place of God's presence. The radiant glory that filled the tabernacle and the temple has its own study (glory), as do the holiness that governed approach to it (holiness) and the sacrifices offered there (atonement).

The Hebrew vocabulary is concrete. The tabernacle is the mishkan, ‘dwelling place’, from the verb shakan, ‘to settle’ or ‘to dwell’; it is also the ohel mo‘ed, ‘tent of meeting’, where God met with Moses. Miqdash, ‘sanctuary’, comes from the root for holiness. Solomon's temple is usually bayit, ‘house’, and its main hall is the hekal, a word that also means ‘palace’ and came into Hebrew through Akkadian from Sumerian, where it meant ‘great house’. The later Jewish word Shekhinah, for God's dwelling presence, comes from the same root as mishkan, but it belongs to rabbinic literature, not to the Bible itself. In Greek, the New Testament distinguishes hieron, the whole temple complex with its courts, from naos, the sanctuary building itself; it was the hieron that Jesus cleared of traders, but it is the naos that Paul says the church is. The tabernacle is skēnē, ‘tent’, and John says the Word “made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14) with the related verb skēnoō, literally ‘pitched his tent’.
ot:
Genesis does not call Eden a temple, but many interpreters have noticed that it is described in the language later used for Israel's sanctuaries. Gordon Wenham's paper Sanctuary Symbolism in the Garden of Eden Story (1986) gathered the evidence. God walks in the garden (Genesis 3:8) with the same form of the verb used for his presence in Israel's camp (Leviticus 26:12; Deuteronomy 23:14). The man is placed there “to cultivate and keep it” (Genesis 2:15), and the same two Hebrew verbs, ‘abad and shamar, are used together of the Levites' duties at the tabernacle (Numbers 3:7-8). Gold and onyx, the materials of the tabernacle and the priest's garments, are found in the land by Eden's river (Genesis 2:11-12), a river flows out of it (2:10), and after the fall cherubim guard its entrance on the east (3:24), as cherubim were woven into the tabernacle's veil (Exodus 26:31) and the sanctuary faced east. G. K. Beale's The Temple and the Church's Mission (2004) developed the theme into a whole biblical theology, and John Walton argued that Genesis 1 itself describes the cosmos as God's temple. Daniel Block, in an essay published in 2013, questioned how much of this Genesis itself intends, arguing that Eden is portrayed as a royal garden more than a sanctuary. On any reading, Genesis begins with God present to humanity and ends its opening chapters with humanity driven out. The patriarchs then meet God at altars, and at Bethel Jacob wakes from his dream to say, “This is none other than the house of God; this is the gate of heaven” (Genesis 28:17).

The exodus has a dwelling place as its goal. Moses sings that God will plant his people on his mountain, “the place, O LORD, You have prepared for Your dwelling” (Exodus 15:17), and at Sinai God commands, “make a sanctuary for Me, so that I may dwell among them” (Exodus 25:8), built “according to the pattern I show you” (25:9). The instructions for the tabernacle (Exodus 25 to 31) come in seven speeches, and the seventh concerns the Sabbath (31:12-17), an arrangement many interpreters read as an echo of the seven days of creation. Between the instructions and the building stands the golden calf, when the presence was nearly withdrawn and Moses pleaded, “If Your Presence does not go with us,” and added, “do not lead us up from here” (33:15). When the work is done, the narrator echoes Genesis 2: “all the work for the tabernacle, the Tent of Meeting, was completed,” Moses sees it and blesses the people, and “Moses finished the work” (Exodus 39:32, 43; 40:33). Then “the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle” (40:34). The tent had a courtyard with the altar and basin, a Holy Place with the lampstand, the table of bread, and the altar of incense, and the Most Holy Place, where the ark of the covenant stood beneath two gold cherubim. God said, “I will meet with you there above the mercy seat” (25:22), so that the ark was his throne or footstool and the tent his portable palace. The covenant's great promise is, “I will make My dwelling place among you” and “I will walk among you and be your God” (Leviticus 26:11-12). In the land the tent stood at Shiloh (Joshua 18:1) until the ark was captured by the Philistines and a grieving mother named her child Ichabod, “The glory has departed from Israel” (1 Samuel 4:21).

David brought the ark to Jerusalem and wanted to build God a house. God answered with a play on the word: David would not build God a house, since “I have moved about with a tent as My dwelling” (2 Samuel 7:6), but God would build David a house, a dynasty, and David's son would “build a house for My Name” (7:13). Solomon began the temple in the fourth year of his reign (1 Kings 6:1), commonly dated around 966 BC, and finished it in seven years (6:38). Its inner sanctuary was a perfect cube, “twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high” (6:20), and its walls were carved with cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers, a stylized garden. At its dedication the cloud filled the house so that the priests could not stand to minister (8:10-11), and Solomon prayed with a theology that refused to shrink God: “Even heaven, the highest heaven, cannot contain You, much less this temple I have built” (8:27). The temple was the place where God set his Name, toward which Israel and even the foreigner could pray and be heard (8:41-43). The Psalms show what it meant to worshipers: “How lovely is Your dwelling place, O LORD of Hosts” (Psalm 84:1); “better is one day in Your courts than a thousand elsewhere” (84:10); “to dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to gaze on the beauty of the LORD” (27:4). Zion was God's “resting place forever and ever” (132:14).

The presence could not be presumed on. Jeremiah stood in the temple gate and warned the people not to chant, “This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD” (Jeremiah 7:4), as if the building guaranteed safety while they oppressed the foreigner and worshiped other gods. He asked, “Has this house, which bears My Name, become a den of robbers in your sight?” and pointed to Shiloh (7:11-12). In exile Ezekiel saw in vision the abominations in the temple and then saw the glory move from the threshold to the cherubim and leave the city eastward (Ezekiel 10:18; 11:23). Nebuchadnezzar's army burned the temple in 587 or 586 BC. Yet Ezekiel heard God promise that he himself had been “a sanctuary for them in the countries to which they have gone” (11:16), and his closing vision (Ezekiel 40 to 48) shows a new temple, the glory returning by the east gate (43:4-5), a river flowing from under its threshold and turning salt water fresh (47:1-12), and a city named “THE LORD IS THERE” (48:35). After Cyrus's decree of 539/538 BC the exiles returned, and prodded by Haggai and Zechariah from 520 BC they rebuilt; the second temple was completed “in the sixth year of the reign of King Darius” (Ezra 6:15), 515 BC. The old men who remembered Solomon's temple wept (Ezra 3:12), and the ark was never recovered. Haggai promised, “The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former” (Haggai 2:9), and Malachi, “the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to His temple” (Malachi 3:1). Isaiah had already called it “a house of prayer for all the nations” (Isaiah 56:7) and had heard God ask, “What kind of house will you build for Me?” (66:1). Between the testaments Antiochus IV defiled the temple in 167 BC, and the Maccabees cleansed and rededicated it in 164 BC, the origin of Hanukkah, the Feast of Dedication (John 10:22). Herod the Great began a vast rebuilding in about 20 or 19 BC, the temple Jesus knew.
nt:
The Gospels present Jesus as the place where God now dwells. Matthew names him Immanuel, “God with us” (Matthew 1:23). John says the Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us, “We have seen His glory” (John 1:14), in language that recalls the glory filling the tabernacle, and Jesus promises Nathanael that he will see angels “ascending and descending on the Son of Man” (1:51), making himself the Bethel where heaven meets earth. As a boy Jesus called the temple “My Father’s house” (Luke 2:49), and throughout his ministry he taught in its courts. When he drove out the traders he quoted Isaiah and Jeremiah: “My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations” and “a den of robbers” (Mark 11:17). Mark frames the act with the cursing of a fruitless fig tree (11:12-14, 20-21), and interpreters debate whether Jesus was reforming the temple or enacting a sign of its coming judgment; E. P. Sanders, in Jesus and Judaism (1985), argued for the second. In John the saying that explains it is, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again,” and John adds, “Jesus was speaking about the temple of His body” (John 2:19-21). The objection that the temple had taken “forty-six years to build” (2:20) fits a date around AD 27 or 28, counting from Herod's start. Jesus claims that “something greater than the temple is here” (Matthew 12:6), tells the Samaritan woman that the hour is coming when the Father will be worshiped “neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem” but “in spirit and in truth” (John 4:21-24), and at the Feast of Tabernacles offers himself as the source of the living water that the Spirit will pour out (7:37-39), taking up Ezekiel's temple river. At his death “the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom” (Mark 15:38).

After Pentecost the presence rests on the gathered people. The Spirit comes with wind and fire and fills “the whole house where they were sitting” (Acts 2:2), and the believers go on meeting in the temple courts (2:46; 3:1), since the first Christians were Jews who honored it. Stephen, on trial for speaking against the temple, quotes Isaiah 66: “the Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands” (Acts 7:48), and Paul tells the Athenians the same (17:24). Paul then applies temple language to the church. “Do you not know that you yourselves are God’s temple, and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16) is addressed to a congregation, and ‘you’ is plural: the church together is the naos. In 1 Corinthians 6:19 he applies the image to each believer's body, which is why sexual sin matters: “your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit.” He strings together the covenant promises of Leviticus 26 and Ezekiel 37 as fulfilled in the church: “we are the temple of the living God” (2 Corinthians 6:16). In Ephesians Jews and Gentiles are being built together into “a holy temple in the Lord” and “a dwelling place for God in His Spirit” (Ephesians 2:21-22), because Christ has broken down “the dividing wall of hostility” (2:14), an image many readers connect with the barrier that kept Gentiles out of the temple's inner courts. Peter calls believers “living stones” being built into “a spiritual house to be a holy priesthood” (1 Peter 2:5).

Hebrews reads the tabernacle as “a copy and shadow of what is in heaven,” quoting God's instruction to Moses to build “according to the pattern shown you on the mountain” (Hebrews 8:5). Christ serves in “the sanctuary and true tabernacle set up by the Lord, not by man” (8:2). He entered “the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood” (9:12), so that believers now have “confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body” (10:19-20). What only the high priest could do once a year, every believer may now do in Christ.

Revelation completes the story. John sees the temple of God in heaven opened and the ark of his covenant within it (Revelation 11:19), and the redeemed serve God in his temple while he spreads his tabernacle over them (7:15). At the end a voice from the throne announces the promise of Leviticus and Ezekiel fulfilled at last: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them” (21:3). The holy city is a cube, like the inner sanctuary of Solomon's temple (21:16), and John says, “I saw no temple in the city, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple” (21:22). The whole city has become the Most Holy Place. A river flows from the throne, as in Eden and in Ezekiel's vision, the tree of life stands on its banks, and God's servants “will see His face” (22:1-4). The Bible that began with God walking in a garden ends with God at home among his people.

keyTexts.why: Eden with its river, gold, and onyx, where the man is set to cultivate and keep the garden; many interpreters read it as the first sanctuary.
Jacob's dream at Bethel, where he names the place the house of God and the gate of heaven, a pattern Jesus applies to himself in John 1:51.
God commands a sanctuary so that he may dwell among his people, built after a pattern he shows Moses.
The completed tabernacle is filled with the glory of the LORD, and the cloud leads Israel through the wilderness.
David wants to build God a house; God promises to build David a house instead, and David's son will build a house for God's Name.
Solomon's dedication prayer confesses that heaven cannot contain God, yet asks him to hear prayer made toward the place where he has set his Name.
The worshiper's longing for God's dwelling place, where one day in his courts is better than a thousand elsewhere.
The temple sermon: the presence of the temple is no guarantee for a people who practice injustice and idolatry, as the fate of Shiloh showed.
A river flows from the renewed temple and brings life wherever it goes, an image taken up in John 7 and Revelation 22.
The Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us, and his glory was seen: the incarnation told in tabernacle language.
Jesus clears the temple and speaks of the temple of his body, which will be destroyed and raised in three days.
The church together is God's temple, indwelt by the Spirit, and so holy that whoever destroys it will be destroyed.
Jews and Gentiles together are being built into a holy temple, a dwelling place for God in his Spirit, with Christ as the cornerstone.
Christ enters the true sanctuary, not made with hands, by his own blood, securing eternal redemption.
The dwelling place of God is with man; the covenant promise of God's presence among his people is fulfilled in the new creation, whose city needs no temple (21:22).

history:
The destruction of the temple by the Romans under Titus in AD 70 shaped both Judaism and Christianity. Rabbinic Judaism, reorganized at Yavneh under Yohanan ben Zakkai, taught that prayer, study of the Torah, and deeds of lovingkindness could take the place of sacrifice; a tradition in Avot de-Rabbi Natan (chapter 4) has Yohanan comfort a disciple at the temple's ruins with Hosea 6:6. The daily prayers were linked to the times of the daily offerings, the Amidah asks for the restoration of the temple service, and the fast of Tisha B'Av mourns the destruction of both temples. After the Bar Kokhba revolt (132 to 135) Hadrian refounded Jerusalem as a Roman colony, and when the emperor Julian allowed the Jews to begin rebuilding the temple in 363, the work was abandoned after fires broke out at the foundations, as the pagan historian Ammianus Marcellinus reported. The Dome of the Rock was completed on the Temple Mount in about 691.

Early Christians read the temple through Christ and the church. Ignatius of Antioch (about 110) called believers ‘temple-bearers’ (To the Ephesians 9), and the Epistle of Barnabas (chapter 16, probably early second century) argued that after the destruction the true temple is the believer in whom God dwells. When Christians began to build churches, they borrowed temple language: Eusebius's sermon at the dedication of the church at Tyre (Ecclesiastical History 10.4, around 315) compared the bishop to Bezalel and Solomon. Medieval Christians built their great churches as images of the heavenly Jerusalem, and Abbot Suger's rebuilding of the abbey church of Saint-Denis near Paris (its choir consecrated in 1144) made light an image of that heavenly city. Yves Congar's The Mystery of the Temple (1958) is a major Catholic account of God's presence from the tabernacle to the heavenly Jerusalem.

The Reformation challenged the holiness of places. The Westminster Confession (1646, chapter 21.6) taught that under the gospel no part of worship is tied to, or made more acceptable by, any place, and many Protestants called their buildings meetinghouses. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries dispensational theology, systematized by John Nelson Darby and popularized through the Scofield Reference Bible (1909), taught that Ezekiel's temple would be built in a coming millennial kingdom, while covenant theologians read the same chapters as fulfilled in Christ and the church. Modern biblical theology renewed the whole subject. Jon Levenson's Sinai and Zion (1985) traced the temple as the meeting of heaven and earth in Israel's faith, Beale (2004) read the entire canon as the widening of Eden's sanctuary until it fills the earth, and Nicholas Perrin, among others, has studied Jesus' own temple claims. The debate over how much of this pattern the biblical authors intended, and how much is the interpreter's synthesis, continues.

differ.view: On Ezekiel's temple: a future temple in the millennial kingdom (dispensational)
differ.body: Ezekiel 40 to 48 gives detailed measurements, a division of the land among the tribes, and regulations for priests, and nothing in the prophecy signals that it should be read as a symbol. It has never been built. It will therefore be built in Christ's thousand-year reign on earth, and the sacrifices offered there will serve as memorials of Christ's death, as the Lord's Supper does now, or as ceremonial purification suited to that age, not as a second atonement. Many who hold this view also expect a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem before Christ returns, reading 2 Thessalonians 2:4 and Daniel 9:27 literally. J. Dwight Pentecost's Things to Come (1958) and John Walvoord are representative.

differ.view: On Ezekiel's temple: fulfilled in Christ, the church, and the new creation
differ.body: The New Testament says Christ's once-for-all sacrifice ended the need for any other (Hebrews 10:12-18), calls Christ's body and the church the temple, and takes Ezekiel's vision up into its own: the river of Ezekiel 47 flows in John 7 and Revelation 22, and the city named ‘The LORD is there’ becomes the new Jerusalem whose temple is God and the Lamb. Ezekiel gave his vision in the language of his own day to promise that God would dwell with his people forever. A rebuilt temple with renewed sacrifices would turn back the fulfillment. Most Reformed, Catholic, Orthodox, and many other Protestant interpreters, including G. K. Beale, hold this view.

differ.view: On church buildings: consecrated sacred space (Catholic, Orthodox, and many Anglicans)
differ.body: God dwells by his Spirit in his people, and precisely because he does, the places where the church gathers to hear the word and celebrate the Eucharist are rightly set apart for him. Solemn rites of dedication consecrate churches and altars, and the building, its art, and its orientation teach the faith and anticipate the heavenly Jerusalem. This is not a return to the Jerusalem temple but an extension of the incarnation, in which God sanctifies material things. The Roman rite for dedicating a church and the Orthodox rite of consecration express this view.

differ.view: On church buildings: the gathered people as the only temple (much of Protestantism)
differ.body: Since Christ is the temple and the church is his body, no building is holier than another, and God is worshiped in spirit and in truth wherever believers meet (John 4:21-24; Matthew 18:20). Buildings are useful and may be beautiful, but treating them as sacred risks drawing attention back to the shadow after the substance has come. The Westminster Confession (21.6) states this, and Puritans, Baptists, Quakers, and many free churches have expressed it in plain meetinghouses and in worship held in homes, halls, and open fields.

errors:
The first error Scripture itself names is presumption: treating God's presence as a possession that guarantees safety whatever the people do. Jeremiah's temple sermon attacks it, and Jesus quotes Jeremiah when he clears the temple. Its opposite is the idea that God can be confined to a place, which Solomon rejected in his dedication prayer and Stephen and Paul rejected before hostile audiences. Christians have also been tempted to speak of the Jerusalem temple and the Jewish people with contempt, as though the temple were merely a failure. The New Testament does not: Jesus called it his Father's house, and the apostles prayed there. The church's confession that Christ fulfills the temple does not license scorn for the people who mourned its loss.

Two errors concern the New Testament's use of the image. One spiritualizes it into disdain for the body, as some Gnostic teachers did; Paul's point in 1 Corinthians 6 is the reverse, that the body matters because the Spirit dwells there and it will be raised. The other individualizes it, reading ‘you are God's temple’ as a statement about private spirituality when Paul addresses a congregation divided by factions and warns that God will destroy whoever destroys his temple. The dwelling of God is personal, but it is never merely private.
life:
The long story of the temple tells believers that God wants to be with them. He did not create the world to watch it from a distance, and he did not rescue Israel only to leave them in the wilderness. That changes prayer. Christians pray with Hebrews' confidence that the way into the Most Holy Place is open through Christ, not with the anxiety of people outside the veil. It also changes ordinary life. If the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, then what is done with it, in sexuality, in work, in rest, in how the sick and the old are cared for, is not beneath God's concern.

The doctrine also gives weight to the gathered church. The congregation, with its quarrels and its weaknesses, is where God has chosen to dwell by his Spirit, and damaging it by division is treated in Scripture as a sin against his house. And it shapes hope. The last pages of the Bible do not describe an escape from the world into a temple in the sky but God's dwelling come down to a renewed earth, where his people will see his face.
questions: Solomon says heaven cannot contain God, yet God fills the temple with his glory. How does Scripture hold together God's presence everywhere and his special presence with his people?
Jesus called his body a temple, and Paul called the church God's temple. What difference does it make that Paul's ‘you’ in 1 Corinthians 3:16 is plural?
Jeremiah warned people who trusted in the temple while they oppressed the vulnerable. What might presuming on God's presence look like in a church or a life today?
